title: Narada: I know only words
hookLine: a learned sage asks to be taken across sorrow
carry: jijnasa: the path of knowing begins with a hunger
tomorrow: a son asks his father what Brahman is. why won't he just say?

cards: Narada again, but in a much older text. In the Chandogya Upanishad, the sage Narada comes to another sage, Sanatkumara, and says: teach me. Sanatkumara answers: first tell me what you already know.
And Narada recites a library. The four Vedas. The old stories.
Grammar, mathematics, the reading of signs, and more. Then the confession. Sir, I know only words.
I don't know the self. I've heard from people like you that whoever knows the self crosses over sorrow. And I am in sorrow.

teach.b: Not after finishing ritual study, Shankara says. Knowing Brahman doesn't depend on that. What comes first is a readiness.
In paraphrase: telling the lasting from the passing; losing the taste for the fruits of action, here or in any heaven; calm and self-restraint; and a longing to be free.
Then therefore: because the scriptures show that what action wins runs out.
Then the last word, jijnasa: not knowing yet, but wanting to know. Many teachers read Narada's confession as that readiness: every book behind him, and now a longing to be free of sorrow.
That's the teaching of the first sutra.

teach.h: THE PATH BEGINS AS A HUNGER.
teach.b: In Vedanta, the path of knowing begins as a hunger, not an answer. Now hold the week up to the light. Priests' wives, with nothing laid over the love.
A king who asked for ears instead of liberation. A mother's rope, two fingers short. A servant boy who caught devotion from the sages.
A hunter climbing to a soft heart. A boy at a cave, asked who he is. And a learned sage, ready at last to begin.
Two paths this week, devotion and knowing, and each says plainly where it stands.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, teachers speak of this readiness, discernment, dispassion, inner discipline and longing for freedom, as what a student cultivates before and during study of the sutras.

o: a reward stored up for the next life
knowledge that starts as a desire to know
the duty to perform rituals perfectly

games.q: the first sutra, word by word. tap the pairs.
p: now: after a kind of readiness
therefore: what action wins runs out
Brahman, the one to be known

s: the first sutra opens with a grand statement of what Brahman is
it opens with a hunger: now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. even learned Narada had to start by asking.
Shankara says knowing Brahman must wait until ritual study is finished
he weighs that guess and answers no; what comes first is a kind of readiness.
jijnasa means wanting to know, not knowing already
the first line is a hunger, not an answer.

games.q: the first sutra begins: now. you're Shankara. after what does this inquiry begin?
o: after readiness: discernment, dispassion, calm, and longing to be free.
after finishing every Vedic ritual and its study.
after a person has already reached full knowledge.
games.why: Shankara reads 'now' as after a kind of readiness, not after ritual study; the desire to know comes when a person is ready.

practice: Many Hindus say an old Upanishad prayer before study or worship, and it sounds a lot like Narada's plea. Asato ma sad gamaya: lead me from the unreal to the real. Tamaso ma jyotir gamaya: from darkness to light.
Mrityor ma amritam gamaya: from death to the deathless. If you pray, say it slowly, once.
If you don't, close your eyes, let one honest question about what lasts rise, and just hold it, the way the first sutra holds the desire to know.

wordCard.voice: Jnana: knowledge that frees. In the first sutra it begins as the desire to know, once a person is ready.

orig.note: Sanskrit jijnasa, the desire to know, from the same root as jnana; the last word of the first sutra.

carryVoice: For the road: jijnasa. The path of knowing begins with a hunger, not an answer. Narada started there. That's the week.

sources.ref: Brahma Sutra 1.1.1 (athato brahma-jijnasa: now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman)

Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.1 (atha as 'after' the fourfold readiness, not after ritual inquiry; atah: scripture shows the fruits of action perish; jijnasa: desire to know, aiming at full realization)
sources.work: Shankara, commentary on the Brahma Sutras (paraphrased)
